strengths: Comprehensive empirical study: the paper evaluates across 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks with a broad set of closed-source, small-scale, and medium-scale baselines, and reports convincing aggregate gains over its InternVL3 base (e.g., average 15.2→45.3 for 2B and 22.3→51.3 for 8B), with a claimed ~+10% margin over embodied-specific competitors like RoboBrain2.0 and Embodied-R1.

The systematic analysis of which VLM data streams transfer to downstream VLA fine-tuning is the most valuable contribution: the finding that out-of-domain embodied reasoning benchmark data does not positively correlate with closed-loop control success, while in-domain (robot-observation) annotated data substantially improves convergence and success rates, is an actionable and non-obvious insight for the community.

Strong practical resources: a 6M-instance modular data engine spanning grounding, spatial, planning, and in-domain simulation data, with a documented generation pipeline (SA-1B masking, BLIP-2 + Qwen2.5-VL captioning/filtering, GPT-4o rollouts in Habitat, SimplerEnv-sourced QA), plus hyperparameters, evaluation sample counts, and stated plans for open-sourcing code, weights, and data.

Interesting scaling analysis (Vlaser-2B better at short-answer grounding; Vlaser-8B better at CoT-heavy planning/simulation), which gives practical guidance on model-size selection for embodied applications.

Reasonable breadth of downstream evaluation on SimplerEnv (WidowX and Google Robot, visual matching and variant aggregation settings), where Vlaser-QA reaches 64.6% avg on WidowX, exceeding π0 (54.9%) and SpatialVLA (42.7%).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in architecture and training: the model is an SFT of InternVL3 with a flow-matching action expert that closely follows π0 (Physical Intelligence, 2025); the core 'synergy' mechanism between reasoning and control is not actually realized — the paper's own results show the reasoning-enhanced Vlaser backbone does NOT improve downstream VLA performance, and gains come instead from in-domain QA data, which somewhat contradicts the framing of 'synergistic embodied reasoning'.

Dataset contribution is largely curation/aggregation of existing public datasets (RoboPoint, ShareRobot, Pixmo-Points, RefSpatial, SPAR, EgoPlan-IT, etc.) plus synthetic annotation; no fundamentally new data modality is introduced, and the heavy reliance on model-generated (Qwen2.5-VL/GPT-4o) annotations raises questions about annotation quality and potential contamination with test distributions.

The central claim of a 'systematic analysis of data effectiveness' is under-supported: only a handful of single-data-stream VLA variants (QA/Spatial/Grounding) on Google Robot, described by the authors themselves as a 'simple ablation' with vaguely reported results ('comparable to the baseline'), no seed/variance reporting for stochastic SimplerEnv success rates, and no statistical significance testing.
No real-robot experiments; all control results are in simulation (Real-to-Sim), which weakens the SOTA claims on WidowX/Google Robot benchmarks.

Some comparative evidence is inconsistent or mixed: on Google Robot variant aggregation, Vlaser(2B) (51.3%) underperforms the plain InternVL3-2B baseline (54.7%), and on several individual WidowX tasks Vlaser(2B) is worse than InternVL3-2B, which complicates the narrative; baseline results are also partly imported from other papers (Lee et al., 2025) rather than re-run under a unified protocol.

Presentation issues: reference errors (e.g., OpenVLA cited as '(OpenAI, 2023)'), duplicated references (Lipman 2023a/b, Li 2024b/c, Gemini Robotics 2025b/c), typos ('aboved', 'Particularlly'), a likely sign error in the flow-matching target u(Aτt|At) = ϵ − At in Eq. 2, and claimed benchmarks (12 listed in caption, 11 enumerated in text) that do not match.

strengths: Broad empirical evaluation: 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks with a large and well-organized set of baselines (closed-source, small-scale, and medium-scale MLLMs), plus closed-loop SimplerEnv evaluation on two embodiments with a reasonable number of evaluation samples (Table 6).

The research question—which upstream VLM data streams actually help downstream VLA policy learning—is timely and relevant; the observation that benchmark gains do not transfer to closed-loop control is a useful negative result for the community.

Substantial engineering effort: a 6M-sample data pipeline (grounding, spatial, planning, in-domain simulation QA) with the construction methodology described in Appendix A.2, and hyperparameters for both training stages are provided, aiding reproducibility.
The model achieves strong aggregate scores on embodied reasoning benchmarks, and the VLA variant is competitive with much larger policies on WidowX tasks despite a 2B backbone.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'synergistic embodied reasoning' is contradicted by the paper's own experiments: the authors state that using Vlaser-2B as the VLA initialization produced 'no clean improvement' over InternVL3-2B, and only the in-domain QA-tuned variant (Vlaser-QA) helps. The headline contribution therefore rests on an essentially negative/obvious finding (in-domain data closest to the target embodiment transfers best), which weakens the paper's framing and significance.

Serious train/test contamination concerns: training data sources overlap directly with evaluation benchmarks (e.g., Pixmo-Points and RefSpatial appear both as Vlaser-6M data sources and as evaluation benchmarks), and Appendix A.2 admits the spatial data is generated 'using the same question template in VSI-Bench.' Without explicit decontamination analysis, the state-of-the-art claims on these benchmarks are not credible.

In-domain QA training data (2M samples) is generated from SimplerEnv—the same simulation framework used for closed-loop evaluation—by an unverified LLM (Qwen2.5-VL-7B). This creates a potential leakage/shortcut concern for the downstream VLA results that is not analyzed or ablated.

Limited novelty: the architecture is essentially a pi0-style design (InternVL3 backbone + flow-matching action expert) applied to an existing backbone, and the data effort remixes many existing public datasets; the 'systematic analysis' amounts to a handful of single-run comparisons (Vlaser vs. Vlaser-QA vs. Vlaser-Spatial vs. Vlaser-Grounding) without seeds, variance, or statistical significance.

Several results are internally confusing or weakly interpreted: the text claims incorporating all data types 'leads to significant improvements, achieving performance comparable to the baseline' (self-contradictory), and Figure 1's 'LiDAR visualization' description is opaque. No clean VLA ablation isolates why Vlaser-QA helps while full Vlaser does not.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: typos ('aboved', 'Particularlly', 'phrases' for 'phases'), a placeholder 'Project Page: Vlaser' link, and imprecise claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art on WidowX' in the abstract while the body reports no gain from the reasoning pretraining that motivates the work).

The practical guidance offered ('shrink the domain gap') is qualitative; there is no actionable analysis (e.g., data mixture scaling, representation probes) explaining the observed transfer failure, limiting the scientific value of the reported insight.

strengths: Comprehensive embodied reasoning evaluation: Vlaser-8B/2B are compared against closed-source (GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and open embodied VLMs (RoboBrain2.0, Embodied-R1) across 12 benchmarks, achieving the best normalized average, which is a concrete and verifiable claim.

The Vlaser-6M data engine is a genuine engineering contribution: systematic curation of grounding, spatial, planning, and in-domain simulation data with a documented generation pipeline (Appendix A.2), and the promise of open-sourcing model, data, and code supports reproducibility.

The systematic study of which VLM data streams transfer to downstream VLA fine-tuning addresses a genuinely under-explored question, and the negative finding (out-of-domain reasoning gains do not correlate with closed-loop control success) is an honest and useful observation for the community.

The architecture is sensible and well-integrated: InternVL3 backbone + flow-matching action expert (π0-style), evaluated at two scales, with reasonable ablations over data streams (Vlaser-QA/Spatial/Grounding) and qualitative rollouts.
weaknesses: The headline narrative ('synergistic embodied reasoning' bridging reasoning and control) is only partially supported by the paper's own results: Table 3 shows Vlaser-2B as a VLA initialization provides no clean improvement over raw InternVL3-2B; gains come mainly from in-domain QA fine-tuning. The core claim of synergy is therefore weaker than advertised.

Potential evaluation contamination for the strongest VLA result: Vlaser-QA is fine-tuned on Bridge/Fractal question-answer pairs generated from SimplerEnv observations (Appendix A.2, Qwen2.5-VL-generated), and then evaluated on the corresponding SimplerEnv WidowX/Google Robot tasks. Training on QA data derived from the same scenes/embodiments as the evaluation risks leaking the evaluation distribution's visual domain, which undermines the 'state-of-the-art on WidowX' claim. A held-out scene/task split or real-robot validation is needed.

No real-robot experiments: all control results are in simulation (SimplerEnv), despite claims about shrinking the 'domain gap to real-world robot embodiment'. Given that SimplerEnv was designed as a proxy, the central conclusion would be much stronger with even a small real-robot study.

Novelty is largely in data curation and re-assembly: the architecture follows prior work (π0-style action expert, InternVL3 backbone, existing public datasets), and much of the analysis confirms what co-training studies (RT-2, π0.5, OpenX) have already suggested. The paper positions itself as 'an initial step', which limits significance.

Ablations are thin: no variance/seed reporting for SimplerEnv rollouts, no ablation of data mixture ratios, action horizon (H=4 seems short), or model scale for the VLA stage (only 2B is studied, while the reasoning results emphasize 8B). The text ablation paragraph is vague ('achieving performance comparable to the baseline') without a table.

Presentation issues: typos ('aboved', 'Particularlly', 'phrases' for 'phases'), inconsistent metric definitions (Table 1 'Avg' normalization is not defined), duplicate references (Gemini Robotics Team cited three times; SimplerEnv cited as two entries), and the figure-1 'LiDAR visualization' caption does not match the radar chart shown.

strengths: Comprehensive data contribution: the Vlaser-6M dataset spans embodied QA, grounding, spatial reasoning, planning, and in-domain simulation data, with a well-documented curation and LLM-based filtering pipeline (including human verification of ~80% judge agreement) described in the appendix.

The systematic study of VLM-to-VLA transfer is the most valuable part of the paper: the finding that out-of-domain embodied reasoning gains (Vlaser-OOD ≈ InternVL3 baseline on SimplerEnv) do not transfer to closed-loop control, while in-domain annotated data yields large gains, is an actionable insight for future embodied VLM/VLA construction.

Broad and reasonably rigorous evaluation: 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks across three model-scale groups, SimplerEnv (WidowX and Google Robot with both Visual Matching and Variant Aggregation), and RoboTwin bimanual tasks, with clear self-comparable ablations (Vlaser-QA/Spatial/Grounding/All vs. Vlaser-OOD) that isolate data contributions.

Strong empirical results: highest average embodied reasoning score among comparable-scale models (~10% margin), state-of-the-art on WidowX SimplerEnv tasks, and consistent gains over the InternVL3 backbone across ablation settings.
Reproducibility commitments (code, data, model weights) and detailed hyperparameter tables (Tables 6-8) support replication.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the architecture is essentially InternVL3 + a pi0-style flow-matching action expert with shared attention; the two-stage SFT recipe follows established practice (pi0, GR00T, SpatialVLA). The contribution is primarily data curation and empirical analysis rather than methodological innovation.

No real-robot experiments; all closed-loop results are simulation-only (SimplerEnv, RoboTwin). Given the paper's central claim about bridging the domain gap to real-world embodiment, the absence of physical-robot validation notably weakens the significance of the domain-gap conclusions.

The main empirical finding (in-domain data transfers better than out-of-domain data) is fairly intuitive; the paper would benefit from deeper analysis of *why* the transfer fails (e.g., representation-level probes) rather than observation-level conclusions.

Some results are under-analyzed or inconsistent: the 2B model outperforming the 8B model on grounding tasks and the weak Vlaser-OOD performance relative to the baseline are noted but not explained; the 8B model is not evaluated in SimplerEnv, so the claimed scaling behavior is not fully substantiated.

In-domain data is generated by Qwen2.5-VL-7B with LLM-as-judge filtering; residual noise and template-driven question diversity may inflate in-domain benefits, and potential bias toward the evaluation distribution is not fully controlled.

Writing and presentation issues: missing project page URL, some awkward phrasing, and claims like 'ultimately attaining the highest overall score' could be stated more precisely given mixed per-benchmark results against RoboBrain2.0 and other strong baselines.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks spanning QA, grounding, planning, spatial intelligence, and closed-loop simulation, which is broader than many prior works.

The systematic analysis of which VLM pretraining data streams (OOD reasoning data vs. in-domain robot-embodiment data) transfer to downstream VLA policy learning is a useful empirical contribution, supported by dedicated ablations (Tables 2-5) covering data types, action chunk length, and sampling steps.
Two model scales (2B and 8B) with clear reporting of baseline groupings (closed-source, small, medium MLLMs), and a stated commitment to release code, data, and model weights, aiding reproducibility.
The data engine is well documented, including the LLM-as-judge filtering pipeline with human verification (~80% agreement), which is more rigorous than typical dataset curation descriptions.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the architecture is a standard InternVL3 backbone plus a flow-matching action expert (essentially the pi0/π0 recipe applied to InternVL3), and the data engine aggregates existing public datasets (RoboPoint, PicoLaVIS, RoboVQA, SPAR, VSLASR, etc.). The core contribution is engineering/data curation rather than a new method or insight, in a crowded space (Magma, RoboBrain, Embodied-R1, SpatialVLA, ChatVLA, VeBrain, MolmoAct).

Circularity concern in the central 'domain gap' finding: the in-domain data is annotated directly on the same SimplerEnv/RoboTwin platforms used for evaluation, so the conclusion that 'in-domain data improves closed-loop success while OOD reasoning data does not' is close to a tautology (train and test distributions match) rather than a surprising insight, and risks inflating the headline results.

Inconsistencies between claims and evidence: the conclusion claims 'state-of-the-art on Bridge', but no BridgeDataV2 results appear anywhere in the paper; abstract claims SOTA on WidowX (supported) and 'competitive' on Google Robot (the Google Robot numbers actually lag several baselines such as GR00T N1.5 and π0). The claim of 'the highest overall score (by +10% margin)' in Sec. 3.1 is contradicted by Table 1, where RoboBrain2.0-7B (57.3) scores higher than Vlaser-8B (51.3).

No real-robot experiments; all closed-loop results are simulation-only, weakening the paper's central claims about bridging the sim-to-real/domain gap between internet-scale pretraining and robot embodiment.

Possible benchmark contamination: several evaluated reasoning benchmarks appear closely related to the training data sources (e.g., grounding data drawn from RefSpatial/RoboSpatial-style datasets while RefSpatial-Bench is an evaluation), yet no decontamination analysis is provided.

The central contribution of the paper (why OOD embodied reasoning gains do not transfer to VLA control) is analyzed only at a superficial level; no mechanistic study, representation analysis, or controlled data-scale experiments are offered to substantiate the 'synergistic reasoning' framing in the title.

Presentation quality issues: Figure 1 caption incorrectly describes a radar chart as a 'LiDAR visualization'; numerous typos and formatting glitches (e.g., 'Alfred' for ALFRED, broken glyphs in the Ethics/Reproducibility statements); the 2B model outperforming the 8B model on simple grounding tasks is noted but not analyzed.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study covering 12 embodied reasoning benchmarks plus three closed-loop control settings (SimplerEnv WidowX, SimplerEnv Google Robot, RoboTwin), with extensive baselines spanning closed-source, small-scale, and medium-scale MLLMs.

The systematic investigation of which VLM pretraining data streams transfer to downstream VLA fine-tuning is the most valuable part of the paper: the finding that out-of-domain embodied reasoning gains (Vlaser-OOD) do not translate to closed-loop control success, while in-domain simulation-annotated data does, is a useful and clearly supported insight (Tables 2-5, Section 3.2), with consistent replication in the hyperparameter ablations (Table 5).

Substantial resource contribution: a 6M-sample curated dataset with a documented data engine (aggregation of public embodied datasets, SA-1B-derived synthetic grounding data, Habitat-based planning rollouts), LLM-as-judge filtering with ~80% human agreement validation, full hyperparameter tables, and a stated commitment to release code, weights, and data.

Strong headline results: +30 average points over the InternVL3 base models on embodied reasoning, and meaningful VLA gains (e.g., 65.1% vs 41.8% on WidowX, 67.5% vs 55.8% on RoboTwin) achieved with an unchanged 2B architecture, isolating the effect of data.
Honest limitations section acknowledging the absence of real-robot experiments, and a clear, readable overall structure.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the benchmark claims: the training data explicitly includes sources that overlap with evaluated benchmarks (e.g., RoboPoint used for training while Where2Place is evaluated; RefSpatial for training while RefSpatial-Bench is evaluated), and Section A.2 states the spatial data was generated 'using the same question template in VSI-Bench.' No decontamination analysis or leakage discussion is provided, so the 'state-of-the-art' embodied reasoning claims in Table 1 are difficult to interpret.

A degree of circularity in the central insight: the in-domain data is generated from SimplerEnv/RoboTwin, the same simulation platforms used for evaluation. The claim that in-domain data improves closed-loop success is therefore partially self-evident (training on data drawn from the evaluation embodiment/visual domain should help), which weakens the generalizability of the 'domain gap' conclusion to real robots — precisely where the paper lacks experiments.

No real-robot evaluation despite framing around bridging VLM reasoning to real-world embodied deployment; all control results are simulation-based (SimplerEnv, RoboTwin), and the real-vs-sim correlation of SimplerEnv is invoked to justify this, but the paper's own conclusion about robot-vs-internet domain shift is exactly the kind of claim that requires real-robot validation.

Limited architectural novelty: the model is InternVL3 SFT plus a pi0-style flow-matching action expert (following prior work); the contribution rests primarily on data curation and analysis rather than methodological innovation, and the 'synergistic embodied reasoning' of the title is not synergistically coupled to control — the reasoning gains demonstrably do not transfer.

Inconsistencies and unexplained anomalies: the abstract claims SOTA on WidowX while the conclusion claims SOTA on Bridge and only 'competitive' Google Robot; Vlaser-2B substantially outperforms Vlaser-8B on point grounding with no analysis; InternVL3-2B beats many stronger VLA baselines on Google Robot visual matching (94.3%), suggesting evaluation setup peculiarities that go unexamined; the project page link is empty.

Several presentation issues: typos ('aboved', ' datas', inconsistent H usage across action-horizon notation between Sections 2.1 and 2.3), duplicate references (Gemini Robotics Team cited twice with identical text; Cosmos-Reason1 under both Azzolini and NVIDIA), and ablation of planning-type in-domain data is folded into 'QA' without separate study, despite planning being advertised as a core capability.
